C90B Pressurization System Overview
Pressurization allows the cabin altitude to remain lower than the aircraft altitude.
This reduces or eliminates the need for supplemental oxygen.
The system provides a breathable cabin environment,
even at high altitudes.
As aircraft altitude increases,
outside air pressure decreases.
Above approximately twelve thousand five hundred feet,
normal breathing is not possible without pressurization.
The system maintains a lower cabin altitude,
creating a pressure difference between inside and outside air.
This is called differential pressure.
The King Air maintains about five point zero psi differential.
This results in a cabin altitude of about six thousand feet at twenty thousand feet,
and twelve thousand feet at thirty thousand feet.
The aircraft is not designed to withstand negative pressure.
The pressurization system works together with the environmental system.
They share ducting to control both pressure and temperature.
The pressurized area,
called the pressure vessel,
extends from the cockpit to the rear cabin.
It is sealed to prevent air leaks.
Pressurization air comes from engine bleed air.
This air is taken from the compressor section of each engine.
It is mixed with ambient air to create a usable airflow.
Bleed air flow is controlled by switches in the cockpit.
If electrical power is lost,
the valves close,
and pressurization is lost.
Air flows into the cabin,
circulates,
and exits through the outflow valve.
This valve controls how much air leaves the cabin.
Controlling outflow controls cabin pressure.
A safety valve provides backup protection.
It prevents overpressure,
allows manual depressurization,
and keeps the cabin unpressurized on the ground.
It also prevents negative pressure during rapid descents.
During takeoff,
airflow increases in stages,
to prevent pressure surges in the cabin.
Cabin pressure is controlled by the pressurization controller.
The pilot selects a desired cabin altitude.
The system then adjusts the outflow valve to maintain it.
The controller has two scales.
Cabin altitude,
and aircraft altitude limit.
These help ensure the system stays within limits.
The cabin altimeter shows actual cabin altitude.
The cabin climb indicator shows the rate of change.
Cabin rate can be adjusted.
Typical rates range from two hundred,
to two thousand feet per minute.
A switch controls pressurization mode.
Press maintains normal operation.
Dump depressurizes the cabin.
Test allows ground testing.
Before flight,
the system should be checked during runup.
Set a lower cabin altitude,
activate test mode,
and confirm pressurization.
Before takeoff,
set the controller to about one thousand feet above cruise altitude.
Adjust the rate for comfort.
In climb,
the cabin altitude increases gradually,
until reaching the selected value.
The system then maintains it.
If aircraft altitude exceeds system limits,
safety valves prevent excessive pressure.
If cabin altitude reaches twelve thousand five hundred feet,
a warning light illuminates.
This indicates oxygen may be required.
During descent,
set the cabin altitude slightly above landing field elevation.
Adjust descent rate for passenger comfort.
The goal is to match cabin pressure with outside pressure at landing.
As the aircraft descends,
the system equalizes pressure automatically.
The cabin becomes unpressurized before touchdown.
Flow control units regulate airflow into the cabin.
They mix bleed air with ambient air,
based on temperature and altitude.
On the ground,
ambient air is limited,
to improve cabin heating.
After takeoff,
ambient air is gradually added,
to prevent pressure surges.
Temperature and pressure sensors adjust airflow automatically.
This ensures stable cabin conditions.
Overall,
the pressurization system is mostly automatic.
The pilot manages settings,
monitors indications,
and responds to warnings.
Proper use ensures passenger comfort,
and safe operation at high altitude.
